name: George Müller

born.place: Kroppenstaedt (Kroppenstedt), near Halberstadt, Kingdom of Prussia (now Saxony-Anhalt, Germany)

died.place: New Orphan Houses, Ashley Down, Bristol, England

life_summary: George Müller was born in 1805 at Kroppenstaedt, Prussia, and grew up in Heimersleben, where his father was a collector of excise. By his own account his youth was marked by theft and debt, including a jail term at sixteen in 1821–22. As a divinity student at Halle he dated his conversion to a Saturday-evening prayer meeting in a private house in November 1825, and in March 1829 he went to London to train with the London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews. After an illness he went to Devon, parted from the Society in January 1830, became pastor of the small Ebenezer Chapel congregation at Teignmouth, and married Mary Groves on 7 October 1830. From May 1832 he ministered with Henry Craik at Gideon and Bethesda chapels in Bristol, founded the Scriptural Knowledge Institution in 1834, opened his first orphan house in Wilson Street in 1836, and between 1849 and 1870 opened five orphan houses on Ashley Down, relying on unsolicited gifts and never going into debt. Mary died in 1870 and in 1871 he married Susannah Grace Sangar; from 1875 to 1892 the couple made preaching tours in Europe, North America, Asia, Africa and Australia while his son-in-law James Wright shared direction of the work in Bristol. He outlived his children, Craik and both wives, continued preaching in Bristol, and was found dead in his room at Ashley Down on 10 March 1898.

phases.label: Prussian childhood and schooling
phases.summary: Grew up in Kroppenstaedt and Heimersleben, where his father collected excise, and was schooled at the cathedral school in Halberstadt and then at the Nordhausen gymnasium (October 1822 to Easter 1825). By his own account these were years of theft and debt, including a jail term in 1821–22.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), ch. I
Dictionary of National Biography, 1901 supplement, 'Müller, George' (Wikisource)

phases.label: Halle divinity student
phases.summary: Studied divinity at the University of Halle, was converted in November 1825 and first preached in August 1826. He sought missionary service, spent time teaching and preaching in Berlin, and was exempted for life from Prussian military service before leaving for England.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), chs. II–III

phases.label: London and Teignmouth years
phases.summary: Trained in London as a prospective missionary to the Jews, then, after an illness, went to Teignmouth, Devon, where he met Henry Craik. He parted from the London Society early in 1830, became pastor of Ebenezer Chapel, renounced a fixed salary, and married Mary Groves in October 1830.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), chs. III–V
Dictionary of National Biography, 1901 supplement, 'Müller, George' (Wikisource)

phases.label: Bethesda and Wilson Street
phases.summary: Ministered with Henry Craik at Gideon and Bethesda chapels in Bristol and founded the Scriptural Knowledge Institution in 1834. From 1836 he ran orphan houses in rented premises on Wilson Street, growing to four houses.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899)
George Müller, A Narrative of Some of the Lord's Dealings, Part 1

phases.label: Ashley Down orphan houses
phases.summary: Directed the orphan work from purpose-built houses on Ashley Down, opening five between 1849 and 1870, while continuing to preach in Bristol. Craik died in 1866; Müller was widowed in 1870, named James Wright as successor that year, remarried in 1871, and from May 1872 Wright shared direction of the work.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), chs. XIII–XVI
Christian History Institute, Timeline (issue 128)

phases.label: Worldwide preaching tours
phases.summary: With his second wife Susannah he made a series of preaching tours in Britain, continental Europe, North America, Asia (including India, China and Japan), Africa and Australia. Between tours he returned to Bristol, where James Wright carried much of the work.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), ch. XVII
G. Fred. Bergin (comp.), Autobiography of George Müller (1905)

phases.label: Final Bristol years
phases.summary: Back in Bristol, he worked mainly for the Scriptural Knowledge Institution alongside James Wright and preached at Bethesda and elsewhere. He was widowed a second time in January 1895 and died at Ashley Down in March 1898.

sources.label: A. T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899), ch. XIX
G. Fred. Bergin (comp.), Autobiography of George Müller (1905), ch. XX

events.event: Born at Kroppenstaedt near Halberstadt, Prussia; before he was five the family moved to Heimersleben, where his father became collector of the excise.

events.event: Aged sixteen, he was arrested at an inn in Wolfenbüttel over unpaid bills and held in prison until 12 January 1822, according to his own account.

corrections: Died place: changed 'Orphan House No. 3, Ashley Down' to 'New Orphan Houses, Ashley Down, Bristol'. Pierson places his apartment in No. 3 but does not say which house he died in; the DNB says only 'found dead in his room'.

Death event: removed 'apparently of heart failure', which no fetched source gives (Pierson says he was found on the floor beside his bed, having apparently felt faint). Changed 'four days after last preaching' to 'four days after preaching at Alma Road Chapel' (6 March 1898), because Pierson says he also attended meetings on 7 and 9 March.
Craik death: made the date precise, 22 January 1866, from Müller's journal in Bergin; attributed 'friend of thirty-six years' to Müller; added the DNB as an independent source (1832–1866 co-worker).

Lydia's death (10 January 1890): the day is not in Pierson or Bergin, so I added Find a Grave (gravestone record) as the source for the date. Bergin is kept as the source for the Jubbulpore news; Pierson citation dropped.

Susannah's death: replaced the unverified claim that 'James Wright' gives 1895 with the DNB (1895). Bergin's compilation heads the entry 1894, though his own words there ('twenty-three years and six weeks' after 30 Nov 1871) fit 1895.
Tours phase: replaced 'the Middle East' and 'East Asia' with Pierson's list (Europe, America, Asia including India, China and Japan, Africa, Australia).
Ashley Down phase: added that Craik died in 1866 and that James Wright was named successor in 1870 (Pierson: 21 months before Nov 1871; CHI timeline).

Life summary: replaced 'taking no collections' (not verified) with 'relying on unsolicited gifts and never going into debt'. Added the January 1830 break with the Society and the 7 October 1830 wedding date. Changed the tour list and the ending to match the verified events.
Jail event: reworded to match Müller's own account (arrested at a Wolfenbüttel inn) and added his Narrative as a source.

Teignmouth pastorate event: added the January 1830 break with the Society (Narrative prints the committee resolution of 27 January 1830); replaced Pierson/Wikipedia-only support with the Narrative and the DNB.
Marriage event: added that Mary was A. N. Groves's sister and that pew rents were given up too (CHI timeline); removed 'sold their possessions', which I did not check.
22 April 1832 event: removed the unverified 'nine-day visit' detail and added the Narrative, which gives the date.
Elijah event: replaced 'fifteen-month-old' with his birth date, 19 March 1834, from Pierson.
SKI event: changed 'began' to 'announced at a public meeting', following Pierson.
Halle phase: added Berlin stay and lifelong military exemption as described by Pierson; dated first sermon to August 1826.
1848 Bethesda event: changed 'circular' to 'letter', following the Brethren Archive's wording.
Added the DNB 1901 supplement as an independent main source and removed Wikipedia from the main source list. Wikipedia is kept only as secondary support for the 1848 division.
